# Climate downscaling using diffusion models

## Introduction
Climate downscaling, transforming a coarse-resolution climate field to a high-resolution climate field, has
gained significance under a changing climate (Ling et al., 2024). A high-resolution
climate field can represent local extremes on a fine scale, giving authorities the opportunity to allocate
their resources more precisely (López-Gómez et al., 2024).

Downscaling is performed either dynamically, utilizing regional climate models, or statistically, by learning a relationship
between coarse and fine climate fields. (Ling et al., 2024) In the last years the application of deep learning methods for 
statistical downscaling has gained increased traction, drawing on the similarity between downscaling and super-resolution of 
natural images (Addison et al., 2022; Merizzi et al., 2024).

In particular the use of diffusion models for downscaling is researched intensively (Springenberg et al., 2026). 
While established approaches focus on modeling a fine-scale climate field deterministically (Ling et al., 2024), diffusion models
make it possible to generate an ensemble of high-resolution climate fields based on a coarse-resolution field, by drawing from
a distribution of high-resolution fields conditioned on a coarse resolution field, (Watt & Mansfield, 2024; Springenberg et al, 2026).

Diffusion models for downscaling have predominantly been evaluated in an idealised setting: The target climate field was 
degraded to a coarse resolution and the subject of analysis was in how well the diffusion model recovers the original resolution
(Merrizi et al. 2024; Watt & Mansfield, 2024). A smaller number of studies apply the trained model to climate projections and assess
how well the climate change signal is preserved (Addison et al., 2025; Aich et al., 2026).

My seminar work incorporates both topics assessed by these papers. More precisely, I train the diffusion model architecture on reanalysis data 
of the Alps, where due to its complex terrain the value added by downscaling is rather large (CITATION). I will investigate the 
two following questions: First, can the diffusion model generate calibrated high-resolution ensembles for temperature and precipitation over the 
Alpine domain? Second, is the model able to preserve the climate change signal when downscaling unseen global warming levels.

## Theory behind climate downscaling using diffusion models
In the context of climate downscaling we want the diffusion model to generate samples drawn from the conditional probability density p(x|y) whereas
y is the context given to the model (input field, orography map and date). We will follow the diffusion-model architecture established by
Song et al., 2021 and refined by Karras et al., 2022, called the EDM-formulation.
The EDM-formulation has beed adopted in several downscaling papers (Watt & Mansfield, 2024; Mardani et al, 2024; López-Gómez et al., 2024) and will also be
the model logic I utilize for my seminar.

Conceptually, the idea of diffusion models is that they generate an image by denoising a Gaussian noise sample iteratively (Song et al., 2021).
The first step to generate training data is by corrupting a high-resolution image $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ by adding Gaussian noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i$ on it. 
This is done for different noise levels $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_i$, that are drawn from a log-normal distribution.
$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}_i &= \boldsymbol{x}_0 + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_i\, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i
&&\text{with } \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I}) &\text{and } \ \boldsymbol{\sigma}_i \sim \mathrm{LogN}(\alpha, \beta^2)
\end{aligned}
$$
The model will now have as a target the clean high-resolution image $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ and as input the corrupted field $\boldsymbol{x}_i$
as well as the low-resolution field $\boldsymbol{y}$, the topography of the field and the date.

The model $D_\theta(x_i; \sigma_i)$ will now be trained so that it estimates the clean field for a given noise level. So now the model is able to estimate a clean image $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0i}$ 
for a given level of corruption of the image.
Now we use the model to generate a high-resolution image. We start off with a sample of gaussian noise and will now iteratively reduce that noise in the image
over many steps. At each step the image (in practice a tensor) is moved into the direction of the clean estimate until the noise level is reduced accordingly.
In the next step the image with the lower noise level will be used as the next input. At the end we have generated a noise-free image over that many steps.
What is now special is that this image generation process is stochastic and not deterministic because each ensemble member starts from an independent 
Gaussian noise draw and we inject at each noise level gaussian noise in the image, which is the stochastic component.
This lets us generate an ensemble of high-resolution climate fields based on the same low-resolution climate field.

As outlined in Figure \@ref(fig:downscaling-workflow) for climate downscaling we first interpolate our coarse field bilinearly, then we compute the residual between
fine-scale field and coarse-scale field. The residual is the target image that we try to generate, after generating a clean residual field we add it on the interpolated field so
we get the downscaled field.

```{r downscaling-workflow, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Residual downscaling workflow: the coarse climate field is bilinearly interpolated to the target resolution, the diffusion model generates the residual, and their sum yields the downscaled field.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("work/13-diffusion_downscaling/figures/model_structure.png")
```

## Data and experimental setup
The data set utilized for this seminar topic consists of two different types of data source.
-- Our data sources will be reanalysis data and climate projection data
-- As mentioned earlier we will perform downscaling on the two climate variables temperature and precipitation
-----  Lopez-Gomez fpr mountaneous terrain => justification to go over the ALps
-- Modelling setup
----- my setup is similar to addison 2025
-- we first train the model on reanalysis data where we coarsen the fine-scaled climate field so the model learns a mapping between coarse and fine resolution. The model is trained on the years 2001 - 2016 validated on
2017 and 2018. After the model has been trained we will apply the trained model on a coarse field from the climate projection data (thanks to A-DROP), to retrieve downscaled version of that field.
